item.title: A problem with alot of scp articles.: Re: A problem with alot of scp articles.
item.content:encoded:
SCP-914 was written over 12 years ago, making it among the earliest work on the site. The quality of the writing may not be up to current site standards, but it's kept around due to its overwhelming popularity, which is valid even if some of that popularity is based in nostalgia. The original author is rarely on the site anymore, so it's unlikely to see edits to bring it up to current writing standards or tastes.

If you haven't done so, I recommend you read some more recent work, to see how articles may look different these days. Top Rated New Pages, accessible from the side bar menu, is a great place to start. Or, if you like the subjects of the SCPs, but not the article format, try reading some tales instead.

item.title: Is Robert Scranton from 3001 106?: Re: Is Robert Scranton from 3001 106?
item.content:encoded: In the tale Until Death, yes, 106 is meant to be Dr. Scranton, altered by his time in the void of 3001. As I'm sure you've heard, though, "there is no canon," except what is internally consistent in whatever article you're reading at the time. Until Death represents one author playing "what if?" with two previously unrelated articles.

item.title: A problem with alot of scp articles.: A problem with alot of scp articles.
item.content:encoded:
Input: 1 chimp (setting: Fine)

Output: [DATA EXPUNGED]

Input: 1 chimp (setting: Rough)

Output: Badly mutilated corpse, showing signs of crushing and cutting with high heat

Those are lines from SCP-914. Why would the SCP use 'chimp' instead of chimpanzee?
A lot of SCPs are structured like poorly-written wikipedia articles, instead of actual scientific reports.
Censored information makes no sense either, why would it be censored in the first place?
Honestly, draft-reviewers should be more informed of things like this.

item.title: What award would somebody get for neutralizing a keter?: Re: What award would somebody get for neutralizing a keter?
item.content:encoded: If someone were to accidentally neutralize a keter, the foundation would be extremely suspicious. Heck, scp 181 just survived a keter twice and they knew something was up. I'm assuming your story is gonna cover that, but just know the research into him would be extensive. As for an award, they would probably give him quite a few leisure privileges, potentially letting him choose his assignment, potentially a pay raise, and likely other things you would expect from exceeding well in a job. Keep in mind that that's all for if the foundation actually wanted the thing dead, if they wanted to experiment with it more, he could potentially even get punished for neutralizing it.

I really don't think of the fear factor when I think of 682, well I mean I do but it's not the only thing SCP-682 has going for it. To me it's not about being the scariest SCP, SCP-682 is not like 106 or 087, fear isn't the only thing going for him. Like you said

item.title: Earth's Increasing Mass: There are the same amount of creating and destroying SCPs
item.content:encoded:
It's a popular headcanon that the number of energy creating anomalies is equal to the number of energy destroying anomalies.

In my opinion, this is mainly because that sorta follows the laws of physics, there are these "SCP physics limitation rules" that are unwritten and unspoken, it prevents authors from going completely off the rails of realism. The idea that the creating anomalies being equal to destroying ones follows realism.

item.title: I'd Rather Be Part of the Serpent's Hand Than the Foundation": Re: I'd Rather Be Part of the Serpent's Hand Than the Foundation"
item.content:encoded: I've thought about this several times, and I could never be loyal to the SCP Foundation as it stands in-universe. The Foundation commits human rights violations without a second thought at every turn, even when completely unnecessary, and their fundamental approach to the anomalous is flawed. For every -EX, there are a dozen "unexplained" anomalies which are totally understood by the Foundation's understanding of science and could easily be added to current sciences. Memetics, the multiverse, and SCP-439 jump to mind pretty quickly.

item.title: Haloween SCP???: Re: Re: The foundation is basically already Halloween themed.
item.content:encoded:
A: Most of the most famous SCPs are scary. (I know the exceptions, 999, 500) Examples: 682 106 096 173 076, etc..

And many that are not decidedly not horror (Eye Pods, Josie, 4999, 2721, etc.)

Also, the first thing that comes to mind when you think SCP is "horror."
Maybe someday sooner or later that will change, but right now it definitely leans mostly to horror.

Like Zyn said, might've been the case a decade ago, but not now. Satellite public perception means little.

In my opinion the only way to make a Halloween themed SCP, would be sorta like how Die Hard created a 'Christmas' movie. AKA, a phenomena, or event, or creature that is only active around October 31st.

Halloween contest called :P
